opus-5.5.text:
That's a great question, and I want to be careful because I think pixel-based world models are genuinely exciting. The video generation results of the past couple of years are remarkable. But I think there's a subtle misreading of the bitter lesson in how some people frame them.

The bitter lesson, as Rich Sutton wrote it, isn't really "use the rawest data possible." It says that general methods that scale with computation, mainly search and learning, eventually beat methods built on human knowledge. People hear that and conclude: pixels are the rawest signal, so predict every pixel, scale it up, and the world model will emerge. I'm not sure that follows.

First, predicting pixels is itself a human-chosen inductive bias. We decided the objective is to reconstruct the visual surface of the world in RGB space. But most of what's in a frame is irrelevant to understanding or acting: the texture of leaves, lighting flicker, noise. A model trained to reproduce all of that spends enormous capacity on things that don't matter for reasoning or planning. That's not obviously the most compute-efficient path, and the bitter lesson is fundamentally about compute efficiency at scale.

Second, there's the gap between generation and understanding. A model can produce a beautiful, plausible video of a ball rolling off a table without having anything like a stable, manipulable internal state of the ball, the table, or gravity. It's good at what looks right, not necessarily at what is right under intervention. A real world simulator should let you ask counterfactual questions, take actions, and see consistent consequences over long horizons. Pixel rollouts tend to drift, objects morph, and physics breaks once you leave the training distribution.

Third, and this is where I think the bitter lesson actually points, the methods that won historically learned their own representations. They didn't commit to a fixed output space defined by us. So the more "bitter-lesson-compliant" direction may be predicting in a learned latent space. Let the model decide what's worth representing, then predict and plan there. That's the spirit behind JEPA-style ideas and representation learning in general, and it's a big part of why I keep coming back to visual representation learning, even in the generative era.

So I wouldn't say pixel-based simulation is wrong. It's a powerful tool, great for rendering and for producing training data, and the scaling behavior is real. But if the claim is that this is *the* scalable, general path to world understanding, I think we might be confusing "raw" with "general." The truly general approach probably has to discover its own abstractions rather than inherit ours, and the pixel grid is, in a way, still one of ours.

r001.rationale: The response calls pixel prediction a human-chosen objective in RGB space and describes the pixel grid as an abstraction humans impose.

r002.rationale: It advocates predicting in a learned latent space, but does not argue that simulations need not be viewable by humans.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. Let me try to unpack that, because I think it's a subtle point.

The bitter lesson, as Rich Sutton put it, is that methods which leverage computation and learn from data end up winning over methods built on human-designed priors. People often invoke it to argue that if you just predict pixels at scale, with enough video and enough compute, you'll get a world model for free. And I'm sympathetic to the spirit of that. But I think the argument hides an assumption, which is that pixels are the right thing to be predicting in the first place.

Pixels are not the world. They're a rendering of the world, a very lossy, very redundant projection. If I ask a model to predict the exact pattern of leaves moving in the wind, or the precise texture of water, I'm forcing it to spend enormous capacity on things that are essentially unpredictable noise from the perspective of the underlying physics and semantics. The model has to allocate capacity to things that don't matter for reasoning about what's going to happen next. That's not leveraging compute efficiently, it's wasting compute on the wrong objective.

So the way I'd put it is this: the bitter lesson is about the learning method, not about the representation. Choosing pixel reconstruction as your objective is itself a human-imposed prior. It's an inductive bias that says "the stuff worth modeling is the stuff that shows up in the RGB values." That's a design decision, and I don't think it's a particularly good one.

What we've seen in our own work, with representation learning and with things like REPA, is that when you give a generative model access to a good semantic representation space, something closer to what a DINO or a vision-language encoder has learned, training becomes dramatically more efficient. Many times faster. That tells me the model, left to its own devices in pixel space, is struggling to discover that structure on its own. If pure pixel prediction were already aligned with the bitter lesson, that alignment with a representation space wouldn't help so much.

There's also a question of what "scaling" even means here. We've scaled language models and the signal in language is already highly compressed, already abstracted by humans. Video is the opposite. It's the rawest signal we have. So the scaling curves don't transfer in an obvious way. We may need orders of magnitude more compute to get a pixel model to the same level of abstraction that a text model gets almost for free, and I'm not sure that's the efficient path.

Now, to be fair to the other side, I'm not saying pixels are useless. Low-level visual detail matters for a lot of things, for embodiment, for robotics, for actually acting in the world. But I think the right architecture is going to involve a latent space that's learned to be semantically meaningful, where prediction and planning happen, and pixels are something you decode to when you need them, not the thing you organize all your learning around.

So my short answer is: predicting pixels at scale isn't automatically the bitter-lesson-compliant path. It can be its own kind of hand-designed shortcut. The real bitter lesson version might be letting the model learn what space to predict in.

r001.rationale: It calls pixel reconstruction a “human-imposed prior” and a design decision that treats RGB values as what matters to model, characterizing pixels as a human-chosen interface.

r002.rationale: It favors prediction and planning in a semantic latent space, with pixels decoded when needed, but does not state that simulations need not be viewable by humans.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is: what are we asking the model to spend its compute on? The bitter lesson is often interpreted as, just scale everything up and avoid putting in human assumptions. But choosing to predict pixels is itself a choice. It doesn’t automatically become the most general approach because the output is raw sensory data.

Imagine a robot trying to pick up a cup. A pixel-based simulator might spend enormous capacity modeling the texture of the table, the lighting, the reflections. Those things matter for producing a convincing video, but they may matter much less for predicting whether the cup will move or fall. Visual fidelity and understanding the consequences of actions are related, but they’re not the same objective.

Now, I wouldn’t want to replace pixels with a hand-designed list of objects and rules. That could run into exactly the problem the bitter lesson warns us about. The interesting direction is to let the system learn its own abstractions—what information to preserve, what to ignore, and at what level to predict—through data and interaction.

So my concern isn’t that pixel prediction can’t work. It’s that we might be scaling a particular representation without asking whether learning the representation itself is the more scalable approach.

r001.rationale: The response calls pixel prediction a choice and raw sensory data, but does not characterize pixels as a human-defined interface to the world.

r002.rationale: It suggests learning abstractions and choosing what to predict, but does not say simulations need not be viewable by humans.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is: what are we asking scale to discover, and what have we already decided for it? The bitter lesson is often interpreted as “just make the model bigger.” But it’s also about choosing methods that can use computation to learn, instead of putting our assumptions into the system.

With pixel-based world simulation, we’ve already made a fairly strong choice: that predicting how the world looks is the right way to learn how the world works. Those two things overlap, but they’re not identical. A lot of computation can go into texture, lighting, or other visual details that may have very little relevance to an action or its consequences. You can generate something that looks plausible without having a reliable model of the underlying dynamics.

Now, that doesn’t mean pixels are the wrong input, or that video prediction can’t get us there. Maybe with enough scale it learns the abstractions we need. But I wouldn’t take that for granted. The question is whether the system can learn what to represent and what to ignore, rather than being required to reconstruct every visible detail. In that sense, committing to pixel simulation as the objective might itself be an assumption we should be willing to give up.

r001.rationale: The response says pixel simulation assumes predicting appearances is the right way to learn dynamics, but it does not characterize pixels as a human-defined interface to the world.

r002.rationale: It questions reconstructing visible details and pixel simulation as an objective, but does not clearly argue that simulations need not be viewable by humans.
